lesson.title: The Manchurian Crisis
lesson.body: In September 1931 an explosion damaged the South Manchurian Railway near Mukden. Japan blamed Chinese soldiers and used the explosion as an excuse to invade Manchuria. China asked the League of Nations for help.

flash.model: The League of Nations' 1932 report on Manchuria. It found Japan's invasion was not self-defence.

practice.question: A jacket costs £40. A sign says 25% off. How much do you pay?
practice.feedback: Right. A quarter of £40 is £10, and £40 − £10 = £30.

source.label: Source A
source.caption: From the Lytton Report, October 1932.
source.text: ‘The military operations of the Japanese troops on the night of 18-19 September 1931 cannot be regarded as measures of legitimate self-defence. The recently established Manchukuo regime cannot be regarded as having resulted from a genuine and spontaneous independence movement; it is an instrument of Japanese policy.’

exam.question: Using Source A, identify two findings of the Lytton Report.
exam.answer: It found that Japan's military action in September 1931 was not legitimate self-defence, and that the new state of Manchukuo was not a genuine independence movement but a tool of Japanese policy.
exam.well: Two findings, each clear and precise.
exam.next: Say what the League did with the report next.
